job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Rafael Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at 7:15 and at Redfield Credit Union in Marston by 8:45. I'm a junior analyst, so I build the monthly loan-book reports, flag late payers and answer questions from the lending team. I studied economics, and this is the first place that lets me use it. I share a two-bed flat with Jonah, a friend from uni, and we split a rent that eats nearly half my pay. Evenings are mostly cooking, a bit of football, and an hour on a spreadsheet of my own debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and an overhyped story. At work I'd tell my manager, Priya, that the assistant I use now and then for drafting emails is fine, but it doesn't change what we do. Online I'd probably stay quiet, because I've seen how fast these arguments get nasty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine about my job but not about my money. My debt is 38,000, and my pay is 24,000, so the loan repayment and rent leave me with barely any buffer. A world where nothing changes also means nothing improves for people like me, and I'd resent that a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try to move up the grade at the credit union within two years. I'd do the evening course in data analysis that Priya suggested, since the credit union may pay half. I'd move 50 a month into a savings pot and keep the football fees, because I don't want my life to be only a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, and a little flat. It's the kind of future where I can plan, which I like, but where the plan is slow and a bit grim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing improves. What would you want to improve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wages for first-job people. I think it's wrong that a degree costs 38,000 and the starting pay barely covers rent. I'd vote for anyone who capped fees or made employers share the cost of training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your spending gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and the monthly football league, in that order. I'd keep the savings pot, even if it's only 30 some months, because the first time I dip into it, I'll never rebuild it.

say: AI is a **useful tool** and an overhyped story, nothing more.
I'd tell Priya (my manager) it helps with **emails** but doesn't change what we do.
think: My job is fine, but my debt is **38,000** and my pay is 24,000, so there's no buffer.
Nothing changing also means nothing improves for **people like me**, and I'd resent that.
do: Aim for the next **grade** at the credit union within two years.
Take the evening **data analysis** course Priya suggested, if the credit union pays half.
Move **50 a month** into a savings pot and keep the football fees.
feel: **Steady** but flat; I can plan, though the plan is slow and a bit grim.

fieldNote: Sees the problem as **entry pay** versus fees, not technology.
Is cautious online; he avoids heated **arguments** he has seen elsewhere.
Wants to keep a little **life** in his budget, football over pure saving.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant to draft emails and report summaries
Take the evening data analysis course with the credit union paying half
Move 50 a month into a savings pot on payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we should plan for it. I'd tell Priya that parts of my reports, the checking and the first draft, can be done by software already. Online I'd back stronger rules on who benefits from the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the first rung is the one that goes. A junior analyst's work is exactly the thinking tasks on that card: checking, summarising, answering simple questions. I'll probably still have a job, but the lending team might hire one analyst where they'd have hired three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean in on purpose. I'd become the person on the team who knows how to run the new tools and check them, so I'm useful. I'd also join the credit-union staff union, which is small but real. And I'd finish the data course and aim at a role that deals with members' problems, which is harder to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not panicked. More like a steady low worry, the way you feel before an exam you've prepared for but that's hard. The debt makes it sharper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd become the person who checks the tools. Why would the firm need that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a tool that's wrong about someone's loan can ruin their month. Someone has to be accountable, and regulators will want a named human. That's a real job, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonah if his job was cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say he can stay on in the flat and we'd work out rent between us for a few months. He works in an estate agency back-office, so he's more exposed than me. I'd rather share a smaller food budget than see him go home to his parents' village.

say: It's real and we should **plan** for it, not pretend.
I'd back stronger **rules** on who gets the savings.
think: The **first rung** goes: checking, summarising and simple questions are my whole job.
The lending team might hire **one** analyst where it would have hired three.
do: Become the team's go-to person for running and **checking** the AI tools.
Join the credit-union staff **union**, small but real.
Finish the data course and aim for a **member-facing** role that's harder to automate.
feel: A steady, **low worry**, like before a hard exam I've prepared for.

steps.text: Learn to run and check the credit union's new loan-report tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is brutal. I'd say governments are asleep and companies will grab the savings before anyone writes a rule. I'd say we need emergency measures, like an income floor and a pause on student loan repayments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the junior analyst job is gone in less than two years, and maybe the whole analyst ladder after it. I'd also worry about the credit union itself. It's a small member-owned place, and bigger banks with AI will undercut it. I'm 22 with 38,000 of debt and under a month of savings, so I've got no real cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything at staying valuable and at covering costs. I'd ask Priya which of the analyst roles will stay, and push the union for a no-redundancy deal for a year. I'd sell my laptop upgrade plan and my bike, and take weekend work at the stadium bars. I'd also look for any public-sector scheme for people displaced by AI, because I don't think a charity will save us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd try to stay useful. I'd be doing sums at night. The scary part is that the sums stop working in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the union could push for a deal. How likely is that really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, to be honest. A small staff union against a global trend is a long shot, but it's better than being alone in the room. If I'm going down, I'd like to have asked first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm OK and I've got a plan. She's a care worker, and she's got her own worries about work. I'd ask her whether care jobs hold up better, and quietly wonder if I should train in something like that.

say: Two years is **brutal** and governments are asleep.
We need an **income floor** and a pause on student loan repayments.
think: The junior analyst job is gone within two years, and the **credit union** itself may struggle.
With 38,000 of debt and under a month saved I have no real **cushion**.
do: Ask Priya which analyst roles will **stay** and push the union for a one-year no-redundancy deal.
Sell my bike and take **weekend** work at the stadium bars.
Look for any public **scheme** for people displaced by AI.
feel: **Scared** but trying to stay useful, doing sums at night that stop working in a year or two.
S2.quote: A small staff union against a global trend is a long shot, but it's better than being alone in the room.
fieldNote: Worries about the **employer** as well as the role: a small mutual against big AI-run banks.
Gets **practical** fast, selling the bike and taking weekend shifts.
Starts wondering about **care work**, prompted by his mother's job.

steps.text: Push the staff union for a one-year no-redundancy deal
Take weekend shifts at the stadium bars
Look for a public scheme for workers displaced by AI
Sell the bike and drop the takeaway budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I'd call a warning, not a reprieve. I'd say to people at work that we should use the time to get rules, funds and training in place, not to panic. And I'd tell anyone who'd listen that the benefits must be shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm anxious but with a real chance. If I stay employed for three years, I can clear maybe half the loan. I'd use that time to move toward the part of finance that stays human, like advising members in trouble, and I'd keep an eye out for anything outside finance too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd split my effort. The first year I'd overpay the loan by 120 a month, because debt is the thing that makes you fragile. I'd finish the data course and also start a part-time certificate in debt advice, which is the human side of lending. And I'd vote and join the campaign for a proper income floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but workable. A kind of seriousness. It's like I've been told the date of a big exam and I can revise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why debt advice rather than something more technical?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people in money trouble want someone who listens, and regulators will want a person signing off. Technical stuff is where the machines will be best. I'd be the person at the desk who explains, and I think that holds longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change plan in year two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the credit union cutting analysts and not replacing them, I'd move faster. I'd apply to the advice charity in the next town and drop the data course. A plan's only good if you're allowed to change it.

say: Five years is a **warning**, not a reprieve; use the time for rules and training.
think: I'm anxious but there's a real **chance**: I could clear half the loan in three years.
The human side of finance, like **advising** members in trouble, holds longer.
do: Overpay the loan by **120 a month** in year one.
Finish the data course, then start a part-time **debt advice** certificate.
Join the campaign for an **income floor** and vote for it.
feel: Tense but workable, like being told the **date** of a big exam.
S3.quote: People in money trouble want someone who listens, and regulators will want a person signing off.
fieldNote: Picks **advice** work over technical work because he thinks machines will beat people at technical tasks first.
Sets clear **triggers** for changing plan, a sign of his steady, evidence-led style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say we have time to do this right if we start. I'd say we need training that pays, fair fees and rules for companies. I'd also say not to treat it as a disaster when it can be a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm cautiously okay. I'd be 32, probably out of debt, maybe with a flat of my own. The thing I'd watch is whether the people in charge really use the decade, or just wait and then say they couldn't have known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on in finance for the first few years and do the debt-advice qualification. I'd save 150 a month once the loan's under control. By year four or five I'd move into member advice or a policy job at a consumer group. And I'd keep using the AI tools, because I'd be good at them by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a wary edge. It's not the sleepless feeling. It's more that I'd be watching the clock on other people's decisions, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wary edge come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From politics, really. I trust my own plan, but I don't trust governments to use ten years well. They'd likely wait until year eight and then panic. That's why I'd stay in the campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about starting a family in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, maybe around 29 or 30, if the income floor and housing are sorted. I'd want some proof that kids won't grow up in a country that left everyone to fend for themselves.

say: Ten years means we have **time** to do this right if we start now.
It can be a **chance**, not a disaster.
think: I'm cautiously okay, probably **out of debt** by 32.
I trust my plan but not governments to use the **decade** well.
do: Do the **debt-advice** qualification and carry on in finance for a few years.
Save **150 a month** once the loan is under control.
Aim for a **member advice** or consumer-group policy job by year five.
feel: Mostly **calm** with a wary edge, watching other people's decisions rather than mine.
S4.quote: I trust my own plan, but I don't trust governments to use ten years well.
fieldNote: Optimism is about **personal** planning; his doubt is about politics.
Brings up **family** plans around 29 or 30, conditional on an income floor and housing.
Would keep **campaigning**, the one thing he can do about government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because it removes the time I need to pay down the debt and move sideways. What would help is a payment pause on student loans, a guaranteed income and employers being made to retrain people rather than drop them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just add that people my age aren't asking for sympathy. We want rules that make sure the gains from AI aren't kept by the same few people who already have the most.

headlineQuote: We want rules that make sure the gains from AI aren't kept by the same few people who already have the most.
portrait: **Rafael** is 22, an economics graduate and junior analyst at a credit union in Marston, sharing a flat.
He has **38,000** of debt, almost no savings and no family money, but he plans carefully and tries things once they're proven.
He leans left, trusts **unions** and rules, and uses AI now and then at work.
He turns each scenario into a **plan**, such as the data course, debt advice and a staff union.
His worry grows with speed: steady at ten years, **alarmed** when only two years' warning.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years removes the time he needs to clear debt and move sideways.
whatWouldHelp: A **pause** on student loan payments, a guaranteed income and employers forced to retrain staff.
Rules that share the **gains** from AI rather than leaving them with a few firms.
